title: Sets and membership
objectives: Describe a set by listing it and by a rule, and use membership and subsets.

screens.title: Multiples of 3
screens.prose: The grid holds the whole numbers from 1 to 20. A number is a multiple of 3 when 3 divides it with nothing left over.
screens.question: Tap every multiple of 3 on the grid.

hints.text: Count up in threes from 3.
3, 6, 9, and keep going while you stay at 20 or below.
The multiples are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. The next one, 21, is off the grid.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count up in threes from 3 and stop at 20.

byKey.digit-3: You added 13 because it has a 3 in it. But $13 = 3 \times 4 + 1$, so 3 does not divide it.
byKey.missed-big: You stopped at 9. 12, 15 and 18 are multiples of 3 too.
byKey.r3c3: 13 has a 3 in it, but $13 = 3 \times 4 + 1$. It is not a multiple of 3.
byKey.r4c5: 20 is $3 \times 6 + 2$, so 3 does not divide it.
byKey.r2c5: 10 is $3 \times 3 + 1$, so it is not a multiple of 3.

explain.text: Counting in threes from 3 gives 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. The next multiple, 21, is past 20. These six numbers are the ones the description picks out.

screens.title: A set
screens.prose:
The numbers you tapped form a **set**, and each one is an **element** of it. We can list it, $A = \{3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18\}$, or give its rule:

$$A = \{n \in \mathbb{Z} : 1 \le n \le 20,\ 3 \text{ divides } n\}$$

$6 \in A$ reads “6 is in $A$”; $7 \notin A$ reads “7 is not in $A$”.
screens.question: $|A|$ is the number of elements of $A$. What is $|A|$?

hints.text: $|A|$ counts elements. It is not the largest element.
Count the shaded cells.
There are six shaded cells, so $|A| = 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many numbers are in the list.

byKey.largest: You gave the largest element, 18. $|A|$ counts how many elements there are.
byKey.twenty: You counted the whole grid. $A$ holds only the shaded numbers.

explain.text: The list $\{3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18\}$ has six entries, so $|A| = 6$. The list and the rule describe the same set.

screens.title: Repeats count once
screens.prose: A set only records what is in it. So order and repeats do not matter: $\{1, 2, 2, 3\}$ and $\{3, 1, 2\}$ are the same set. On the grid, shading 2 a second time changes nothing.
screens.question: What is $|\{1, 2, 2, 3\}|$?

hints.text: Which different numbers appear in the list?
The 2 is written twice. Is it in the set twice?
The elements are 1, 2 and 3, so the size is 3.

feedback.correct: Right. The set has three elements: 1, 2 and 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the different elements, not the entries written.

byKey.repeat: You counted the 2 twice. A set holds each element once, however often it is written.

explain.text: Writing 2 twice does not put it in the set twice. The elements are 1, 2 and 3, so $|\{1, 2, 2, 3\}| = 3$.

screens.title: A set inside a set
screens.prose: Let $S$ be the multiples of 6 from 1 to 20. The shaded cells are $A$, the multiples of 3.
screens.question: Tap every element of $S$.

hints.text: Count up in sixes from 6.
6, 12 and then one more before 20.
$S = \{6, 12, 18\}$. The next multiple, 24, is off the grid.

feedback.correct: Right. $S = \{6, 12, 18\}$, and every one of them is shaded.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count up in sixes from 6.

byKey.all-a: You tapped all of $A$. Only every second multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6.
byKey.r1c3: 3 is in $A$, but 6 does not divide 3.
byKey.r2c4: 9 is in $A$, but $9 = 6 + 3$, so 6 does not divide it.
byKey.r3c5: 15 is in $A$, but $15 = 12 + 3$, so 6 does not divide it.

explain.text: $S = \{6, 12, 18\}$, and each element of $S$ is also in $A$. When every element of one set lies in another, the first is a **subset** of the second: $S \subseteq A$.

canvas.caption: $S \subseteq A$: every element of $S$ is in $A$

screens.title: An interval is a set
screens.prose: An interval is a set of real numbers: $[0, 1) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : 0 \le x < 1\}$. As in Equations, the filled dot at 0 keeps 0 in. The hollow dot at 1 leaves 1 out.
screens.question: Tap every point that is an element of $[0, 1)$.

hints.text: An element must satisfy $0 \le x < 1$.
Check the two ends: is $0 \le 0$? Is $1 < 1$?
0, 0.25 and 0.75 are in. 1 fails $x < 1$, and −0.5 and 1.5 are outside.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each point against $0 \le x < 1$.

byKey.with-1: You included 1. The hollow dot means $1 \notin [0, 1)$, since $1 < 1$ is false.
byKey.no-0: You left out 0. The filled dot means $0 \in [0, 1)$, since $0 \le 0$.
byKey.p5: 1 is not in the set: $1 < 1$ is false.
byKey.p1: −0.5 is below 0, so it fails $0 \le x$.

explain.text: The rule is $0 \le x < 1$. It keeps 0, because $0 \le 0$, and drops 1, because $1 < 1$ is false. So $0 \in [0, 1)$ but $1 \notin [0, 1)$.

screens.title: Every subset
screens.prose: A subset of $\{a, b, c\}$ is any set built from its elements, including none or all of them. For each element we choose in or out.
screens.question: Count the subsets of each size, then the total.

hints.text: Read each row of the list and count.
The empty set is one subset of size 0.
$1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8$. Two choices for each of 3 elements also gives $2^3 = 8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each row of the list, then add.

byKey.r0c1: Size 0 has one subset: $\varnothing$. It counts, even though it has no elements.
byKey.r4c1: Add the four counts: $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8$. Leaving out $\varnothing$ gives 7.
byKey.r1c1: There is one subset for each single element: three.
byKey.r2c1: Choosing two of three elements gives three pairs.

explain.text: Each element is either in or out, so there are $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^3 = 8$ choices. Each choice gives one subset. Choosing out for all three gives $\varnothing$.

screens.title: In, or inside
screens.prose: $\in$ joins an element to a set. $\subseteq$ joins a set to a set. Here $B = \{1, 2, 3\}$.
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: You read $\in$ as $\subseteq$. The elements of $B$ are 1, 2 and 3; the set $\{2\}$ is not one of them.
You used $\subseteq$ with a number on the left. 2 is an element, not a set, so write $2 \in B$.

hints.text: For $\in$, ask: is the left side one of the listed elements?
The listed elements of $B$ are 1, 2 and 3, all numbers.
$2 \in B$ and $\{2\} \subseteq B$ are true. $\{2\}$ is a set, not one of the numbers listed.

feedback.correct: Right. 2 is an element of $B$, and the set $\{2\}$ is a subset of $B$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what kind of thing sits on each side of the symbol.

byKey.setin: You chose $\{2\} \in B$. That says the set $\{2\}$ is listed in $B$, but only numbers are listed.
byKey.numsub: You chose $2 \subseteq B$. $\subseteq$ needs a set on the left, such as $\{2\}$.
byKey.in: You left out $2 \in B$. 2 is one of the listed elements.
byKey.sub: You left out $\{2\} \subseteq B$. Its only element, 2, is in $B$.

explain.text: $2 \in B$ because 2 is listed. $\{2\} \subseteq B$ because every element of $\{2\}$ is in $B$. But $\{2\} \in B$ is false: the set $\{2\}$ is not one of the listed elements.

screens.title: What subset means
screens.prose:
You checked $S \subseteq A$ element by element. That is a for-all statement, as in For all and there exists:

$$X \subseteq Y \Leftrightarrow \forall x\ (x \in X \Rightarrow x \in Y)$$

Two sets are **equal** when each is a subset of the other. $\varnothing$ is the set with no elements.
screens.question: Is $\varnothing \subseteq A$, where $A$ is the multiples of 3?

options.text: Yes. No element of $\varnothing$ is outside $A$
No. $\varnothing$ has no elements, so none of them is in $A$
options.why: You looked for an element in $A$. The for-all fails only if some element of $\varnothing$ is outside $A$, and there is none.

options.text: No. $\varnothing \in A$ is false, so $\varnothing \subseteq A$ is false
options.why: You mixed $\in$ with $\subseteq$. $\varnothing$ is not listed in $A$, but it is still a subset.
Every set has $\varnothing$ as a subset, empty or not.

feedback.correct: Right. The for-all is vacuously true, so $\varnothing$ is a subset of every set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would make $\forall x\ (x \in \varnothing \Rightarrow x \in A)$ false.

explain.text: To break $\varnothing \subseteq A$ we need an element of $\varnothing$ outside $A$. There is none, so the for-all holds vacuously, as in If, then. So $\varnothing \subseteq X$ for every set $X$.

screens.title: Proving a subset
screens.prose: Claim: every multiple of 6 is a multiple of 3. In sets, $\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : 6 \text{ divides } n\} \subseteq \{n \in \mathbb{Z} : 3 \text{ divides } n\}$. The grid showed it up to 20; a proof must cover every integer.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x$ be any multiple of 6, so $x = 6k$ for some integer $k$.
So $x$ is a multiple of 3. As $x$ was any multiple of 6, the subset holds. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: An example checks one element. The for-all needs an arbitrary multiple of 6, so the proof starts from $x = 6k$.

hints.text: A subset proof starts with an arbitrary element of the smaller set.
Write that element using the definition, then rewrite it.
Let $x = 6k$; then $x = 3(2k)$; so $x$ is a multiple of 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from any multiple of 6, rewrite it, then conclude.

byKey.d1: You kept the example $12 = 3 \times 4$. It checks one number; the proof must work for any $x = 6k$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. All three general lines belong.
byKey.s2: Rewrite $x$ only after you have written $x = 6k$.

explain.text: We took any multiple of 6, $x = 6k$, and wrote it as $3(2k)$. Because $k$ was arbitrary, the argument covers every multiple of 6. One example, such as 12, covers only itself.

screens.title: Why that line holds
screens.prose: The middle line said $x = 3(2k)$, “and $2k$ is an integer”. Without that, $x = 3(2k)$ would not show $x$ is a multiple of 3.
screens.question: Why is $2k$ an integer?

options.text: $2$ and $k$ are integers, and a product of integers is an integer

options.why: You used what we are proving. That 3 divides $x$ is the conclusion, so it cannot be a reason.
You fixed $k$. Then the proof covers only $x = 12$; $k$ must stay arbitrary.
That is true, but it is about $x$, not $2k$. It does not show $2k$ is an integer.

hints.text: What do we know about $k$?
$k$ is an integer by the definition of a multiple of 6.
$2$ is an integer and $k$ is an integer, and multiplying integers gives an integer.

feedback.correct: Right. $2k$ is a product of two integers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use only what the first line gave us about $k$.

byKey.circ: You assumed 3 divides $x$. That is the goal of the proof, not a step towards it.

explain.text: The first line says $k$ is an integer. A product of integers is an integer, so $2k$ is one. That is exactly what “multiple of 3” asks for.

screens.title: A stock screen
screens.prose: A stock screen returns a set. Six stocks from a FTSE 100 universe (names and figures invented). Screen 1 keeps $\{s : \text{P/E of } s < 10\}$. Screen 2 adds “yield above 5%”.
screens.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Screen 1 returns Avonmore, Bridgegate, Dunmore and Fenwick
Screen 1 sorted by P/E and sorted by name give the same set
Screen 2's output is a subset of Screen 1's
Re-sorting the output changes the set
options.why: You treated the order as part of the set. A set records only which stocks are in it.

options.text: Screen 2 can return a stock Screen 1 rejects
options.why: You let the extra filter add stocks. Every stock Screen 2 keeps already passed P/E below 10.

hints.text: Apply the rule P/E below 10 to each row.
Avonmore 6.8, Bridgegate 8.9, Dunmore 7.5 and Fenwick 9.7 pass.
Screen 2 keeps Avonmore, Bridgegate and Fenwick, all already in Screen 1's output.

feedback.correct: Right. Order does not matter, and an extra filter gives a subset.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find Screen 1's set first, then compare.

byKey.diff: You picked re-sorting as a change. The same four stocks are in, so it is the same set.
byKey.more: You let Screen 2 add a stock. A stock must pass both tests, so it passed the first.
byKey.list: You left out the list. Those four have P/E below 10.
byKey.sort: You left out the re-sort. Order does not change a set.
byKey.subset: You left out the subset. Screen 2's stocks all pass Screen 1.

explain.text: Screen 1 is $\{$Avonmore, Bridgegate, Dunmore, Fenwick$\}$, in any order. Screen 2 is $\{$Avonmore, Bridgegate, Fenwick$\}$. Every stock it keeps passed Screen 1, so it is a subset.

ideas: A set is described by a list or by a rule. Order and repeats do not matter: $\{1, 2, 2, 3\} = \{3, 1, 2\}$.
$x \in X$ says $x$ is an element; $X \subseteq Y$ says every element of $X$ is in $Y$. $\{2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$, but $\{2\} \notin \{1, 2, 3\}$.
To prove $X \subseteq Y$, take an arbitrary $x \in X$ and show $x \in Y$. A set of $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, $\varnothing$ among them.

formula.name: Subset
formula.tex: X \subseteq Y \Leftrightarrow \forall x\ (x \in X \Rightarrow x \in Y)

summary.trap: $\in$ takes an element on the left and $\subseteq$ a set: $2 \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $\{2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$.

quiz.prose: $\{\varnothing\}$ is the set whose one element is the empty set.
quiz.question: What is $|\{\varnothing\}|$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the entries between the outer braces.

byKey.zero: You counted the elements of $\varnothing$. The outer set holds one thing: the empty set itself.

explain.text: A box holding an empty box is not empty. $\{\varnothing\}$ has one element, so $|\{\varnothing\}| = 1$, while $|\varnothing| = 0$.

quiz.question: Which equal $\{1, 2, 3\}$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You treated a subset as equal. 3 is missing, so $\{1, 2, 3\} \not\subseteq \{1, 2\}$.
You let an extra element in. 4 is not in $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Order and repeats do not change a set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements.

options.why: You read $n \le 20$ as $n < 20$. 20 is allowed, and 5 divides it.
You wrote the size of $F$ as its only element. $|F| = 4$, but $F$ holds four numbers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each number against both conditions.

explain.text: The rule keeps the integers from 1 to 20 that 5 divides. That is 5, 10, 15 and 20. 0 fails $1 \le n$, and 20 passes $n \le 20$.

quiz.prose: A desk can trade any subset of four products: rates, FX, equities and credit, including none.
quiz.question: How many subsets are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each product is in or out.

byKey.no-empty: You left out $\varnothing$, trading nothing. It is a subset too.
byKey.three: You used $2^3$. There are four products, so $2^4$.
byKey.four: You counted the single products only.

explain.text: Each of the four products is in or out, so there are $2^4 = 16$ subsets. That includes $\varnothing$ and the whole set.
